decisions.quote:
In three experiments, subjects named pictures with low or high-frequency superimposed
distractor words. In a first experiment, we replicated the finding that low-frequency words
induce more interference in picture naming than high-frequency words (i.e., distractor frequency
effect, Miozzo & Caramazza, 2003).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings classify this study as a replication. Primary evidence confirms that Dhooge and Hartsuiker collected new experimental data from Dutch-speaking participants (Experiments 1-3) using Dutch stimuli to re-test the distractor frequency effect in picture-word interference originally reported by Miozzo and Caramazza (2003).

corrected_value.title: Now you see it, now you don’t: On turning semantic interference into facilitation in a Stroop-like task.

decisions.location: Experiment 2, Results and discussion (lines 555-562); see also Experiment 2 introduction (lines 425-429), Experiment 2 discussion (lines 579-582), and References (lines 893-894)
decisions.quote:
We
introduced a control condition, in which distractors and picture were semantically related. If
distractors are not processed under masked conditions, no effect should be found with
semantically related distractors either. However, a semantic facilitation effect was present. As
stimuli were presented under the same masking and timing parameters in both conditions, it
seems unlikely that the same subjects could only process the distractors when they were
semantically related to the target. Also, the same semantic facilitation effect was found by
Finkbeiner & Caramazza (2006) who used the same presentation parameters as we did.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Experiment 2 (N = 40 Dutch speakers), Dhooge and Hartsuiker empirically retest the finding of Finkbeiner and Caramazza (2006) that picture-word interference with semantically related vs. unrelated distractors produces semantic interference when distractors are visible but reverses into semantic facilitation when distractors are masked using the same presentation timing parameters. Experiment 2 tests the relatedness by visibility interaction (F1(1,39) = 26.62, p < .001; F2(1,19) = 17.57, p < .001), confirms both visible semantic interference and masked semantic facilitation, explicitly compares the finding with Finkbeiner and Caramazza (2006), and states that 'by replicating the semantic facilitation effect, this experiment also provides further evidence for a non-competitive model of lexical selection.' The reference list (lines 893-894) identifies the primary study as 'Finkbeiner, M., & Caramazza, A. (2006). Now you see it, now you don’t: On turning semantic interference into facilitation in a Stroop-like task. Cortex, 42, 790–796.' (distinct from the 2006b reply commentary on lines 895-896), with no DOI printed in the source text. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 663, 10.1037/0096-3445.132.2.228, Miozzo & Caramazza, 2003, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 132, 228-252) represents the unmasked distractor-frequency original retested in Experiment 1 (sibling target_index 0). Because Finkbeiner and Caramazza (2006) is an independent study in Cortex testing a different empirical phenomenon (masked reversal of semantic interference into facilitation), report equivalence does not apply and the target is genuinely absent from the shipped rows. Luna's invalid table-formatted duplicate_quote was discarded and replaced with a verified contiguous primary-source quote preserving exact line breaks.
